title: How do you configure Hibernate for efficient JDBC batch inserts? What do hibernate.jdbc.batch_size and order_inserts do, and why must you avoid IDENTITY generation?
shortTitle: What are JDBC batch insert configuration settings?

s1_definition.profdef: JDBC batching groups many INSERT/UPDATE statements into a single round trip to the database instead of one round trip per statement. You enable it with `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` (the number of statements per batch). `hibernate.order_inserts` and `hibernate.order_updates` reorder pending statements so those targeting the same table are adjacent, which is required for them to actually batch together. You must avoid `GenerationType.IDENTITY` for ids because identity columns force Hibernate to execute each INSERT immediately to read back the generated key, which disables batching entirely; use `SEQUENCE` (with a pooled allocation size) instead.
s1_definition.analogy: Sending one statement per round trip is like a courier driving to the bank and back for every single document — exhausting and slow. JDBC batching is loading fifty documents into the van and making one trip. The batch size is how many documents fit in the van. Ordering inserts is sorting the documents so all the ones for the same department are bundled together, otherwise the courier keeps switching bundles and cannot batch them. Using an identity column is like a rule that every document must be hand-stamped with a number at the counter the moment it arrives — so the courier can never load a full van; they must present each document one at a time.
s1_definition.oneliner: batch_size groups statements per round trip; order_inserts/order_updates make same-table statements batch together; IDENTITY ids force one insert per row and kill batching, so use SEQUENCE.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** JDBC batching groups many INSERT/UPDATE statements into a single round trip to the database instead of one round trip per statement. You enable it with `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size` (the number of statements per batch). `hibernate.order_inserts` and `hibernate.order_updates` reorder pending statements so those targeting the same table are adjacent, which is required for them to actually batch together. You must avoid `GenerationType.IDENTITY` for ids because identity columns force Hibernate to execute each INSERT immediately to read back the generated key, which disables batching entirely; use `SEQUENCE` (with a pooled allocation size) instead.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Sending one statement per round trip is like a courier driving to the bank and back for every single document — exhausting and slow. JDBC batching is loading fifty documents into the van and making one trip. The batch size is how many documents fit in the van. Ordering inserts is sorting the documents so all the ones for the same department are bundled together, otherwise the courier keeps switching bundles and cannot batch them. Using an identity column is like a rule that every document must be hand-stamped with a number at the counter the moment it arrives — so the courier can never load a full van; they must present each document one at a time.

**One line to remember:** batch_size groups statements per round trip; order_inserts/order_updates make same-table statements batch together; IDENTITY ids force one insert per row and kill batching, so use SEQUENCE.

sections.s2_technical:
Without batching, Hibernate sends each INSERT as its own JDBC execute, so inserting 10,000 rows means 10,000 network round trips — dominated by latency, not by the database's actual insert speed. `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size = 50` tells Hibernate to accumulate up to 50 statements and send them with JDBC's `addBatch`/`executeBatch`, cutting round trips by up to 50x.

```yaml
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size: 50
```

But batching only works when consecutive statements are the *same* prepared statement (same table, same columns). If your action queue interleaves inserts into different tables — account, then holding, then account, then holding — JDBC cannot batch them because the prepared statement keeps changing. `hibernate.order_inserts = true` reorders the queued inserts so all account inserts are grouped, then all holding inserts, letting each group batch. `hibernate.order_updates = true` does the same for updates.

```yaml
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts: true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates: true
```

The IDENTITY problem is fundamental. With `GenerationType.IDENTITY`, the primary key is generated by the database (an auto-increment/serial column) and is only known *after* the row is inserted. Hibernate must read that key back immediately to populate the entity, so it is forced to execute each INSERT the moment you persist — it cannot hold statements to batch them. The result: batching is silently disabled no matter what batch_size you set.

`GenerationType.SEQUENCE` fixes this because Hibernate can fetch id values from the sequence *before* inserting, so it knows the ids up front and can defer and batch the inserts. A pooled allocation size (`allocationSize = 50`) means Hibernate grabs 50 ids per sequence call, cutting sequence round trips too.

```java
@Id
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "g")
@SequenceGenerator(name = "g", sequenceName = "account_seq", allocationSize = 50)
private Long id;
```

Senior nuances and extras: on PostgreSQL add `reWriteBatchedInserts=true` to the JDBC URL so the driver rewrites batched inserts into a single multi-row INSERT for a further speedup. Combine batching with the flush+clear pattern so memory stays bounded. Set `hibernate.generate_statistics=true` to verify batches are actually forming. Batching and `@DynamicUpdate` can conflict because dynamic updates produce varying SQL that cannot batch. And `@Version` optimistic locking is still honored in batched updates, with batch failures reported appropriately.
sections.s3_banking:
**Problem 1 — a transaction-history backfill took hours because of per-row round trips.** At National Bank of India, backfilling millions of historical transaction rows ran one insert per round trip, and network latency made it crawl. Enabling batch_size collapsed the round trips. This is exactly what batch_size fixes.

**Problem 2 — batching did nothing until ids and ordering were fixed.** Even with batch_size set, the TransactionRecord used IDENTITY ids, so Hibernate inserted one row at a time; and parent/child inserts interleaved. Switching to SEQUENCE and enabling order_inserts finally let the batches form. This is exactly the IDENTITY and ordering pitfall.

What the code will do: a `HistoryBackfillService` inserting TransactionRecords with SEQUENCE ids, the config enabling batch_size and order_inserts, PostgreSQL `reWriteBatchedInserts`, and statistics on to prove batches form.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: 100,000 transaction amounts, batch_size 50.

Step 1 — before inserting, Hibernate fetches a block of 50 ids from the sequence in one call (pooled allocation), so it already knows the ids for the next 50 rows without touching the table.

Step 2 — the loop persists records. Each persist assigns a pre-fetched id and queues an insert; no SQL runs yet because SEQUENCE lets Hibernate defer.

Step 3 — after 50 persists, `flush()` sends those 50 inserts. Because order_inserts grouped same-table statements and batch_size is 50, JDBC packs them into one batch; with `reWriteBatchedInserts`, PostgreSQL folds them into a single multi-row INSERT — one round trip for 50 rows.

Step 4 — `clear()` detaches the batch to keep memory flat, and the loop proceeds. Had the id used IDENTITY, each persist would have forced an immediate single insert and no batch would ever form.

Step 5 — a final flush handles the remainder, commit finalizes, and the statistics log shows far fewer prepared-statement executions than rows, proving batching worked.

```
2026-10-24 01:22:40 INFO  Backfill done: 100000 rows; prepared statements=2000, flushes=2000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  backfill(100,000 amounts)   batch_size=50, SEQUENCE ids
    │
    ▼
  seq call → 50 ids pre-fetched (pooled)
    │
  LOOP persist → id assigned, INSERT queued (no SQL)
    │
    ├─ every 50 ──→ flush()
    │                order_inserts groups same-table INSERTs
    │                JDBC addBatch×50 → executeBatch → ONE round trip
    │                (reWriteBatchedInserts → single multi-row INSERT)
    │               clear() → bounded memory
    ▼
  final flush → COMMIT
  stats: ~2000 statement executions for 100,000 rows (50x fewer round trips)

  ── IDENTITY variant ──
  persist → MUST insert now to read key → 100,000 round trips → no batching
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — JDBC Batch Insert Config (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Batch/Chunk processing; pooled id allocation               │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────┐
  │  O: performance tuned via config, not by rewriting logic    │
  │  S: service inserts; id strategy/config handle efficiency   │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Config Roles (as prose) ──
  jdbc.batch_size=N : accumulate N statements per JDBC round trip.
  order_inserts     : group same-table inserts so they can batch.
  order_updates     : same for updates.
  SEQUENCE + allocationSize : ids known pre-insert → defer + batch.
  reWriteBatchedInserts (PG): fold a batch into one multi-row INSERT.
  generate_statistics: confirm batches actually form.

  ── Why IDENTITY breaks batching (as prose) ──
  IDENTITY key is DB-generated and known only AFTER insert, so Hibernate
  must execute each insert immediately to read it back → cannot hold
  statements → batching silently disabled regardless of batch_size.

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. seq → pre-fetch ids (pooled)
  2. loop persist → queue inserts
  3. every N → flush → JDBC batch → one round trip
  4. clear → bounded memory → final flush → commit

  (Caution) IDENTITY disables batching. (Caution) @DynamicUpdate varies SQL → can't batch.
  (Caution) match loop batch to jdbc.batch_size. Rule: SEQUENCE + batch_size + order_inserts.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
JDBC batching groups many insert or update statements into a single round trip to the database instead of paying network latency for every single statement. I enable it with the Hibernate JDBC batch size property, which tells Hibernate to accumulate that many statements and send them together using the JDBC batch API, and for a large load that can cut round trips by the batch-size factor, turning a job that took hours into one that takes minutes. But batching only works when consecutive statements use the same prepared statement, so if the action queue interleaves inserts into different tables, nothing batches. That is what the order inserts and order updates properties fix: they reorder the queued statements so all the inserts for one table are adjacent and can batch as a group.

The most important pitfall is identity generation. With an identity primary key the value is generated by the database and is only known after the row is inserted, so Hibernate is forced to execute each insert immediately to read the key back, which means it can never hold statements to batch them, and batching is silently disabled no matter what batch size I configure. The fix is sequence generation, because Hibernate can fetch id values from the sequence before inserting, so it knows the ids up front and can defer and batch, and a pooled allocation size lets it grab many ids per sequence call to cut those round trips too.

At National Bank of India a transaction-history backfill of millions of rows was crawling because it did one insert per round trip, and even after I set the batch size, nothing improved because the records used identity ids and parent and child inserts interleaved. Switching the id strategy to a sequence with a pooled allocation size, enabling ordered inserts, and on PostgreSQL adding the rewrite-batched-inserts flag so the driver folds a batch into a single multi-row insert, finally let the batches form, which I confirmed by turning on Hibernate statistics and seeing the statement count drop far below the row count. The nuances I always mention are that I pair batching with the flush and clear pattern so memory stays bounded, that dynamic update conflicts with batching because it produces varying SQL, and that I match my loop's batch size to the configured JDBC batch size so each flush sends a full batch.

---

keyPoints: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50: group 50 INSERTs into one JDBC batch
hibernate.order_inserts=true: group by entity type for batching
IDENTITY generator BREAKS batching — use SEQUENCE instead
